s01.slug: MONDAY · 8:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK
body: The Fishbowl TV is on CNN with the sound turned down to a murmur, and in Berlin it’s already dusk. The picture is blue and gold: the Brandenburg Gate lit up like a wedding cake, and running away from it along the line where the Wall used to stand, a mile of giant foam dominoes, each one taller than a man and painted by somebody’s schoolkids — flags, faces, a dove, a fist, a Trabant with flowers growing out of the tailpipe. Every one of them still standing. The crawl says they go over tonight. Tonight in Berlin is a little before lunch here.

Jack is at the front desk for his mail, which is a postcard from Driftwood Books about a sale and nothing from Ohio, when Priya Raman comes around the end of the counter with her clipboard against her chest and a pink envelope riding on top of it.
“Costigan.” She holds it out. “Housing sends the RAs the hold list, and I’m supposed to *facilitate a conversation*.” She doesn’t let go of her end right away. “This is me facilitating.”

body.title: RESIDENTIAL SERVICES — NOTICE OF BALANCE DUE
body.text:
SPRING 2010 HOUSING · COSTIGAN, JOHN A. · DELGADO 412
Balance after aid: $340.00
A REGISTRATION HOLD has been placed on your record. Payment or an approved arrangement is due at Residential Services by 5:00 p.m., Friday, November 13.

body: Jack knows the number before he’s finished reading it. It’s the part of spring that was going to come from Glenwood Avenue, back when there was SUB pay for it to come from.

“Your registration window is Monday at seven a.m.,” Priya says, off the clipboard, although she doesn’t need the clipboard. “Hale’s spring seminar fills by seven-oh-five. I’m not telling you that to stress you out. I’m telling you because it’s on a spreadsheet.” She clicks her pen. “Also. The Brick’s circulation desk lost two overnight people to the swine flu. Midnight to six. Eight-forty an hour.” The pen clicks again. “I’m not *recommending* it. I’m informing you it exists.”
“Is there a form for being informed?”
“There’s always a form,” Priya says, and goes back behind the desk to inform a girl in a Pi Lam sweatshirt about her mini-fridge.
Up on four, Margot has been at the lounge whiteboard before breakfast, in black marker, in capitals that could cut glass:

body.title: 4th-floor lounge whiteboard
body.text:
20 YEARS · WHO BROUGHT IT DOWN?
(DISCUSS. ARGUE. BE WRONG.)
TONIGHT 9 P.M.
In the corner the useful-idiots tally: C 8 · B 7, and under it, in Margot’s smallest capitals, STUPAK: SAME SIDE (BOTH).

body: Jack reads it on his way past with his bag on one shoulder. In 412 he takes Hale’s reader out of the bag, folds the pink envelope in thirds along the creases Housing already gave it, and slides it in at Hume, at the part about miracles, and closes the reader on it.

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists.

body: The sun is far enough down to come through the blinds sideways, and 412 is striped with it. Jack has had the post open on the Dell for half an hour and hasn’t answered it. The Newman desk closes at five; Becca’s lab lets out at six; there is a procedure, and he is not allowed to open the box without her, and it’s a box from her mother. He sits and looks at the word *mom* in lowercase.

Theo is at the espresso machine, which is the most expensive object in Delgado Hall, pulling himself a shot in a cup the size of a thimble. Theo doesn’t look for things. Things turn up for him. He lifts Hale’s reader off the corner of Jack’s desk to use as a saucer, and the pink envelope slides out of Hume onto the blotter and falls open, and Theo reads it the way he reads everything left within six feet of him: all at once, without moving his head.
“Three hundred and forty dollars,” he says.
“Doesn’t matter.”
“Costigan, I spend that on *parking*.”
“No.”

Theo looks at him over the little cup. Then he folds the envelope back along its creases, slides it into the reader at Hume where it was, and squares the reader to the corner of the desk exactly the way it sat before his espresso came anywhere near it. He drinks the shot in one swallow, standing.
“The offer,” he says, “has no expiration date.”

Then he’s across the room and flat on his bed with his shoes on the duvet and last week’s *Variety* open over his face like a pup tent, and the only sound in 412 is the espresso machine on the shelf, ticking to itself as it cools.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 1:04 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The RAZR goes off on the desk at two minutes past one, loud enough against the wood to lift Theo’s head off his pillow, and the little outer screen lights blue in the dark: MOM. It is two minutes past four on Glenwood Avenue.

Jack has it open before the second buzz and is out the door in his socks. In the east stairwell the one bar of reception lives on the third step up from the fourth-floor landing. He stands on it with his free hand on the cold rail.
“Jackie.” His mother is very calm. That’s how he knows.

She lays it out in order, the way she reads the parish announcements. The SUB pay ended last week; he knew that. Last night his father went down to the bar on Midlothian for the Monday game — “the *Steelers*, Jack, your father, who spits when they come on” — and the bar closed at two-thirty, and it’s four, and the truck isn’t back. His cell phone is on the counter beside the sugar bowl. She’s looking at it.

Nonna is up. She got dizzy on the stairs Sunday and has been sleeping in the chair, and she’s at the kitchen table now with her beads; Jack can hear them on the oilcloth. Gina’s up too, his mother says, sitting on the stairs, where she thinks nobody can see her.
“I’m not calling the police on your father, Jack.” A breath. “I’m calling you.”

He sits down on the third step with the phone hard against his ear and the cinderblock cold through his T-shirt. The stairwell light buzzes over him. Twenty-four hundred miles, and from here there is one thing he can do: stay on the phone.

choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You prayed the Sorrowful Mysteries with her until the truck pulled in.
response: “Ma. Let’s pray it.”

So they do. It’s already Tuesday in Youngstown, so it’s the Sorrowful Mysteries, and the Agony in the Garden comes first, which is about right. His mother leads from the kitchen phone and Jack answers on the third step with his forehead against the rail, and under the second decade Nonna comes in from across the kitchen in Italian, half a line behind them, *Santa Maria, Madre di Dio*, slow and low and sure of every word. They get through the Crucifixion. His mother goes back to the top without asking, and Jack answers.

At 1:51 — ten to five on Glenwood Avenue — his mother stops in the middle of a word. Headlights, across the kitchen window. Then Jack hears it himself from the far side of the country: the garbage can at the curb going over, and the lid going down the driveway on its rim, ringing. “He’s home,” his mother says. “Go to sleep, honey.” And then, because it’s ten to five and she is his mother and there is still a list: “The spring thing. For your room. We’ll find it.”

“I’ve got it, Ma.” The screen door; her slippers on the back steps. A minute later her voice comes back from out in the driveway, quiet, with the cold in it. “He says he sat in the lot at Lordstown. To see if the lights were on.” Nobody’s hurt. The can has a dent in it. She hangs up to go bring him in.

choices.text: Talk to her about anything else.
choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You talked her through it — Rosie’s crabs, the cardoons — until the truck pulled in.
response: “Ma. Tell me about Rosie’s crabs.”

She knows what he’s doing, and she lets him. Rosie has drawn thirty-some crabs since Becca’s card came, most with the wrong number of legs, and taped them up the cellar door in rows. Then the cardoons: nobody in Ohio sells a cardoon in November, she gets them off Mr. Pallante’s cousin, who grows them behind the Sunoco, and it’s a saga, and she tells all of it. Then Becca’s stationery — are those Holsteins, she wants to know, or the brown ones — and Jack says he’ll ask. She talks for forty minutes about nothing, and the whole time he can hear her watching the window.

choices.text: “Ma. What did he say before he left?”
choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You asked what he said before he left: “Don’t wait up.”
response: It takes her a second. “He said, ‘Don’t wait up.’” The kitchen clock ticks in Ohio. “Twenty-six years, Jack. He’s never said that. He always says what time.”
After that there isn’t much to say, so they don’t. She tells him when a car comes down Glenwood, and when it doesn’t slow, and he sits on the step and listens to her listen.

s05a.slug: TUESDAY · 2:06 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, THE LANDING WINDOW
body: The landing window is open its six inches, and the night coming through it is dry and mild and doesn’t move. Jack has the Reds out of the Carhartt’s inside pocket. He went back to 412 for the jacket at some point and has no memory of the trip.
He stands at the window with the pack in his hand. He doesn’t open it, and he doesn’t put it back.

In Youngstown it’s after five. His father is in the house by now, or in the garage with the space heater, and his mother is making coffee because there’s no sense going to bed, and Gina’s bus comes at ten to seven. Down below, the sodium light over the Anacapa lot is the color of weak tea, and past it the eucalyptus along Ocean Road stand in the light without a leaf going.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · MISSION STREET POST OFFICE
body: The Mission Street post office has one window open at twenty to four and a line of six, and the sun comes in sideways through the high windows over the PO boxes and makes bright squares on the linoleum that people step around without meaning to.

When it’s his turn he fills out the form at the counter with the pen on the bead chain. PAY TO: D. KOSTELNIK. STRUTHERS, OH, the street from memory. FROM, nothing. Twenty dollars. “Dollar ten for the fee,” says the clerk, and Jack pays twenty-one ten out of his wallet in a ten and a five and the rest in singles, and all the while the pink corner of the Residential Services envelope sticks up out of Hale’s reader in the bag at his feet.
The stub goes behind his Mooney ID with the other two.

Outside, Rafi Ochoa is sitting on the curb with his skateboard across his knees and a flat-rate box beside him on the sidewalk, addressed in fat black Sharpie to his abuela in OXNARD, CA. He looks up. His eyes go to the wallet as Jack puts it away, to the stub going in behind the ID, and back up to Jack’s face, and that is all he does about it.
“No stress, boss.”
He gets up and brushes off his board shorts. “You need work?” He says it like the price of a burrito. “I got an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.”
Jack looks at him.
“*Vitamins*, boss.” Rafi looks a little wounded. “Not bars. I don’t do bars.”

He holds out his hand for the receipt — the customer’s copy, D. KOSTELNIK, $20.00 — and Jack gives it to him. Rafi turns it over on his knee and writes his number across the back with the Sharpie off his abuela’s box, in big careful numerals, and hands it back. Then he picks up the box, tucks the skateboard under his other arm, and shoulders through the door to mail it, holding it on his way for an old woman with a cane.

journal.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)
journal.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike on the wharf at one in the morning like it was nothing, till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says. Outside the post office he offered me an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 5:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE NEWMAN LOUNGE
body: At half past five the Newman lounge has the end-of-day light it gets from the Grove side, the sun low through the blue glass so the old couches look like they’re at the bottom of a pool. The box is on the coffee table: Priority Mail, an Idaho return address, enough packing tape to hold a barn together. Becca is cross-legged on the carpet beside it with her pocketknife already open.
“Sit,” she says. “I open, you watch. That’s how we do it at home. Whoever it’s for watches.”

She slits the tape in three clean strokes and lays the flaps back. On top is a letter on the cow stationery — it’s Mrs. Lindell’s stationery too, it turns out; the cows run in the family — and Becca hands it to him and watches him read the first line, which is *Dear Jack*, and the second, which has *boyfriend* in it, underlined once in blue ballpoint. Under the letter there’s a cookie tin with a poinsettia on the lid, a month early, and under that a pair of gray wool socks thick enough to stand up by themselves.
“North Idaho socks,” Jack says. “My feet are in *California*.”
“That’s what they’re for.” She doesn’t explain, and it isn’t a joke.
Last, wrapped in a dish towel, two jars of huckleberry jam, purple-black, with masking-tape labels in her mother’s Sharpie. The first says JACK. The second says FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE.
“She knows he exists,” Becca says. “She doesn’t know he’s — whatever Theo is. I didn’t want to write that letter.”

Jack moves Hale’s reader off the table to make room for the jars, and the pink envelope slides out of Hume onto the carpet face up. Becca picks it up to hand it back and reads it on the way — not snooping; she reads everything the way she reads the ear tag on a stray, once, all the way through, so she knows whose it is. She gets to HOLD and stops.
She folds it on its crease and gives it to him. Then she sits back on her heels and thinks, the way she thinks about anything, in a straight line from one end to the other.

“I have six hundred and twelve dollars,” she says. “From Daisy.” He doesn’t know who Daisy is. “My market heifer. Four-H, last year. She was a very good heifer.” Her chin comes up a little. She means every word of it. “It’s in my checking. I can get it out tomorrow.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind.

choices.text: Take her hand. “Keep Daisy. I mean it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You took her hand and told her to keep Daisy.
response: He takes her hand. There’s a nick across the middle knuckle, healing, from something with hooves. “Keep Daisy,” he says. “I mean it.”
Becca looks down at their hands. “Okay,” she says. She doesn’t take the hand back, and she doesn’t take the offer back either. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

That night in 412 Theo receives the second jar with both eyebrows. He turns it to the desk lamp, reads the label, and looks at Jack over the lid. “I’m a supporter,” he says, “not a member.” Then he clears a place for it on the shelf beside the espresso machine, label out, and steps back to see how it looks there.

choices.text: “I can’t accept a cow. My mother would hear about it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You told her you couldn’t accept a cow.
response: “I can’t accept a cow,” he says. “My mother would hear about it.”
“She’s not a cow anymore. She’s a *deposit slip*.” But Becca laughs, and lets him have his no. She just won’t take the offer back along with it. “It’s there. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

response: “I can’t take your heifer, Becca.”
She nods once, the nod she’d give an auctioneer. “Okay.” She folds the knife against her thigh and puts it away and closes the flaps of the box. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 9:40 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE DISH PIT
body: The Hobart runs ninety seconds a load — the long hiss, the shudder, the door coming up on its own steam — and on the shelf over the flat-top Rudy’s transistor has KNX turned low, traffic on the 405 for people who aren’t on it. Jack racks plates and tells it like a joke.
“Guy on my floor offered me two hundred bucks to ride a shoebox down to the wharf.”
Rudy doesn’t turn around from the flat-top. He presses a patty with the back of the spatula and listens to it. “I know what an errand is, mijo.”
He says nothing else for an hour. The Hobart says plenty.

Gloria comes back from the walk-in with a crate of lemons on her hip and the cold still coming off her apron, sets the crate on the steel by Jack’s elbow, and starts counting the tip jar into her palm. Halfway through she stops. Hale’s reader is wedged on the shelf over the dish sink behind the Comet, with a pink corner sticking out of it that says HOLD in its little window. She doesn’t pull it out. She doesn’t need to.
“Advance against December,” she says, low. “Don’t tell Rudy, he’ll want one.”
“I’m okay, Gloria.”
“Hon.” That’s her whole argument. Then she lets him, and picks up the lemons, and takes them out front.
At 10:44 the RAZR goes in his apron pocket, and again, and again.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’

response: He thumbs it out with the dish water still on his hands, a letter at a time.

response: Four minutes of nothing. The Hobart, twice. Rudy’s radio gives the weather for the Grapevine.

choices.text: Set the alarm for 3:50 and call her before school.
response: He doesn’t text back. He sets the RAZR’s alarm for 3:50, and at 3:50 he takes it out to the east stairwell and calls her: ten to seven on Glenwood Avenue, before school. Gina picks up before it has finished ringing once and says almost nothing — *yeah*, and *i know*, and *ok* — and he talks, and she listens to him talk until he hears her bus.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 1:10 AM · THE ANCHOR, UNDER THE HOBART
body: At ten past one the Anchor’s kitchen is down to one fluorescent tube over the dish pit and Rudy scraping the flat-top in long, patient strokes, the grease going into the trough. Out front Gloria has the chairs up. The Hobart’s door is open and the last of its steam is going up into the hood.

Jack gets down on his knees on the wet tile and reaches under the machine, behind the drain line, where the Folgers can has lived since September with its plastic lid on. He takes it out and counts it once, on the steel, under the light.

body.text: One hundred fifty-four dollars. The ANCHOR envelope is in a St. Vincent de Paul basket, and that’s where it should be.

body: The hold is three hundred and forty.

body.text: *Your penance is to let somebody help you this week.* It’s Thursday.

body: Behind him Rudy knocks the scraper twice on the edge of the trough and goes on scraping.

choices.text: Call Rafi. One ride, two hundred.
choices.key: Thursday you ran Rafi’s errand. Two hundred dollars, folded once.
response: He takes the money-order receipt out of his wallet and dials the number off the back of it. Rafi answers on the second ring like it’s noon. “Boss.” Jack tells him Thursday, and Rafi says come by 204 at a quarter to two, he’ll have the box. Behind Jack the scraper stops. Then it starts again.

choices.text: Let Theo. It goes on the tab.
choices.key: You let Theo pay the hold. It’s on the tab.
response: He texts it with the dish water still on his thumb: *ok. on the tab.* The answer comes back before he’s got the lid on the can, because Theo doesn’t sleep.

response.text: Residential Services opens at 9. I’ll wear a blazer.

choices.key: You took the night desk at the Brick and Priya’s hardship extension.
response: He texts the number on the door of 401: *night desk still open?* Priya is awake at ten past one, because Priya is always awake at ten past one.

response.text: Res Services 9AM. Bring ID. Do NOT be late. There is a form.

body: The harbor at a quarter past two is all glare, clear and mild, the water hammered flat, the sea lions on the float barking at nothing in particular. The Vans shoebox rides on La Flaca’s rack under two bungee cords. Rafi handed it over at the door of 204 at a quarter to two, taped shut on every seam, and it’s heavier than shoes.

Jack takes Mission down to the wharf at the speed of a man with sneakers in a box. He is coasting past the Anchor when the door opens and Ray Ochoa comes out with a coffee to go, in the windbreaker, his sunglasses pushed up on his head.
“Saint Isidore.” Ray lifts the cup. His eyes go to the bike — his son’s bike — and to the box on the rack. “New shoes?”
“My roommate’s.”
“Big feet, your roommate.”

Ray doesn’t look at the box again, and he doesn’t follow. When Jack looks back from the end of the wharf the detective is sitting sideways in the open door of the Crown Vic with his coffee, facing the water.

The Wharf Rat’s back door is propped open on an empty keg. A man in a Padres cap Jack has never seen takes the box without a word, goes in, and comes back out with two hundred dollars in twenties, folded once.

At 3:55, at the Residential Services window, Jack puts down the hundred and forty out of the Folgers can — the can under the Hobart is nearly empty now — and Rafi’s two hundred, still folded once. The clerk counts it and taps at her keyboard, and the screen turns her face green. HOLD RELEASED. She asks if he wants a receipt. He takes it, and folds it, and puts it in his wallet behind the Mooney ID with the other papers he keeps there.

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. The hold’s paid. A hundred forty out of the can and two hundred from Rafi’s errand. A shoebox to the Wharf Rat’s back door.

journal.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)
journal.text: Detective Sergeant, per the badge wallet. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter: Tuesdays, meatloaf, a nod to Rudy. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property. Thursday on the wharf: ‘Saint Isidore. New shoes?’ He didn’t look in the box.

s11b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:05 AM · RESIDENTIAL SERVICES, THE WINDOW
body: At five past nine there are eleven people ahead of them, most of them in pajama pants, under fluorescent light and a poster of a cartoon pelican that says DON’T LET YOUR HOUSING GO BELLY-UP. Theo makes twelve. He is in a navy blazer at nine in the morning. For Theo, this is an event.
“Poppy has a thing,” he says, when Jack looks at the blazer, and leaves it there.

At the window he lays a card on the counter. It is black and heavier than a card has any business being, and the clerk picks it up and holds it to the light before she swipes it, and looks at Theo, and looks at her screen. Three hundred and forty dollars goes through without a sound.
“It’s not charity, Costigan,” Theo says, signing. “It’s an investment in my roommate situation.”
“It goes on the tab.”
“There’s no need for a —”
“The tab, Theo.”
Theo sighs at the ceiling tiles, takes back the receipt, turns it over on the counter, and uncaps his pen. He writes on the back in his small square capitals and hands it across.

Jack stands at the window with it and lets somebody help him. It is harder than it looks. It looks like nothing at all — a boy in a blazer and a slip of paper — and the clerk is already calling the next pair of pajama pants.
“Peach,” Theo says. “Not the Anchor’s. Yours. Find somebody to teach you.” He checks the Submariner. “La Cañada. I’m late for a cheese plate.”

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. The hold’s paid. Theo, at the window, in a blazer. The tab: $340.00, plus one pie (peach).

body: Priya is waiting outside Residential Services at nine o’clock exactly with a coffee she hasn’t touched and the Brick’s lanyard still around her neck from the night shift. She holds out a form in a plastic sleeve.
“Hardship extension,” she says.

It’s filled out. All of it, in her small upright hand: his name, his student ID, his permanent address on Glenwood Avenue, and in the box marked REASON, which allows two lines, *Change in family financial circumstances*, with a footnote. It has been laminated.
“Per Section 4.2,” Priya says. “I need the sleeve back.”

At the window the clerk reads the form, looks at the lamination, and looks up at Priya. “Oh,” she says. “It’s you.” Ten minutes later the hold has been moved to December first, pending payroll, and the clerk has stopped looking at the lamination.

“The night desk,” Priya says on the way out, walking fast. “Tonight and tomorrow. Midnight to six. Eight-forty an hour. You check things in, you check things out, you wake people up at five-fifty, and you do not let anybody into the stacks with soup.” She holds out her hand, and he puts the empty sleeve in it. She looks at the sleeve, and at him.
“Don’t make me regret informing you.”
She goes off across the Commons toward the Brick with the coffee still untouched and the sleeve under her arm.

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. Hardship extension to December first, laminated. The night desk at the Brick: midnight to six, eight-forty an hour.

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Filled out my hardship form before I asked. Laminated. She wants the sleeve back.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 10:32 PM · MISSION STREET → THE 11 BUS
body: On the sidewalk outside Bastille the string lights are still on over the door, and the 11 is coming down Mission with its sign lit. Julian has his guitar case in one hand. He turns to Lena with the other hand in his pocket and asks it gently, the way you’d ask permission for something much smaller.
“Can I walk you back?”
“Yes,” Lena says.
“Lovely set, Julian,” says Laney, perfectly. Her pink BlackBerry is in her hand, and its screen stays dark.

On the bus Jack and Laney take the back seat. Lena and Julian sit three rows up with a guitar case’s width between them, and the 11 goes down Mission past the dark Borders and out Ocean Road with every window rattling. At the Anacapa stop the two of them get off first. On the curb Laney takes Jack’s arm and turns him the other way round the Lagoon.
“Walk me home, fireman,” she says. “Apparently I’m available.”
Across the black water, far ahead, Delgado’s front door opens on its square of yellow, and two people go into it, and then there’s no square.

body.text: The Brick, 11:55, the night desk: a returns cart; three grad students asleep on their arms; at 1:45 the lights blink once for the custodians. Eight-forty an hour and nobody asks him anything.
body.else: Across the dark Commons the Brick’s second floor is lit, the way it’s lit every night.
